tasks.task_description: Build a traffic-flow model of the four Washington corridors (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520) that relates lane count, peak traffic volume, and the penetration fraction of cooperating self-driving vehicles to corridor throughput, then determine how the network responds as AV share rises 10% -> 50% -> 90%.
tasks.task_analysis: Data preparation: the supplied CSV has 224 milepost segments on four routes; columns were stripped of stray whitespace, the BOM was handled via utf-8-sig, and the Comments column (201 of 224 missing) is metadata only. One I-5 segment (MP 172.58-172.98) lists 6 lanes in one direction against 5/5 neighbours and a fleet-wide maximum of 4 per direction; it was treated as a data-entry error and dropped (1/224, 0.4% of segments; dropping it changes no route-level conclusion). All milepost chains are continuous, so segments are independent capacity units. Model form: a static, segment-wise, two-state flow model. Expert exchange 1 established the decisive structural fact: stop-and-go breakdown is triggered when peak flow reaches about 80-90% of capacity and, once entered, is a *persistent* (metastable) equilibrium - so each segment carries a free-flow branch and a stop-and-go branch, not a smooth curve. The capacity of the free branch scales with a heavy-vehicle adjustment and, under AV penetration f, with a platoon gain g(f) = (G-1)*m*f^2, where the f^2 law comes from expert exchange 3 (a vehicle only rides in a tight platoon when its neighbours are also cooperating, so the benefit scales with the square of the cooperative fraction and saturates as f -> 1; exchanges 2 and 3 together say the theoretical ceiling is 1.5-2x human throughput but the realistic mixed-traffic realization is a 30-70% gain). This is a sound method because it reproduces the two empirically observed regimes (healthy flow below the threshold; persistent waves above it), uses only parameters with stated empirical provenance, and is transparent enough to answer every sub-question numerically.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per segment s with L_s lanes (sum of both directions) and 2015 average daily traffic A_s: C_lane = 2000 veh/h (free-flow lane capacity; exchange 5, interval [1800, 2000]); C_H = C_lane/(1 + p_h*(f_h - 1)) = 2000/(1 + 0.06*1.0) = 1887 veh/h (human-traffic lane capacity, p_h = 0.06 heavy-vehicle share [0.05, 0.08], f_h = 2.0 passenger-car equivalent [1.5, 3.0], exchange 7); g(f) = (1.7 - 1)*0.5*f^2 = 0.35*f^2 (platoon gain, ceiling 1.7x [1.5, 2.0] and mixed-traffic realization 0.5 [0.3, 0.7], exchanges 2-3); C_L(f) = C_H*(1 + g(f)); C_s(f) = C_L(f)*L_s (segment free-flow capacity, vph); V_s = 0.10*A_s (peak-hour volume, K-factor 0.10 [0.08, 0.12], exchange 4); VFC_s(f) = V_s/C_s(f). State rule (exchange 1): segment is FREE if VFC_s < theta = 0.85 [0.8, 0.9], otherwise STOP-AND-GO; in the SAG state the segment passes only C_BKD = 1500 veh/h per lane [1400, 1700, exchange 9], so effective capacity E_s = C_BKD*L_s in SAG, C_s(f) in FREE. Route-level metrics: mean VFC, percent of segments in SAG, mean effective capacity. Parameter table (name = value, interval, source): C_lane = 2000, [1800, 2000], source: expert exchange 5; theta = 0.85, [0.8, 0.9], source: expert exchange 1; C_BKD = 1500, [1400, 1700], source: expert exchange 9; K-factor = 0.10, [0.08, 0.12], source: expert exchange 4; p_h = 0.06, [0.05, 0.08], source: expert exchange 7; f_h = 2.0, [1.5, 3.0], source: expert exchange 7; G = 1.7, [1.5, 2.0], source: expert exchange 2; m = 0.5, [0.3, 0.7], source: expert exchange 2; free-flow speed = 60 mph interstates / 55 mph SR-520, source: expert exchange 8. Computation: python code/model.py, one run per f in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}, logs in logs/model_sweep.log and logs/sensitivity.log.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (f = 0): all four corridors are already over capacity at the peak hour in the model. Mean directional V/C: I-5 1.21, I-90 0.82, I-405 1.43, SR-520 0.93; 86% of I-5 segments, 87% of I-405, 60% of SR-520 and 48% of I-90 sit in the persistent stop-and-go state. This matches the expert's field observation (exchange 10) of near-daily peak-direction breakdown on these corridors. Effect of AV penetration: (i) I-5: V/C falls 1.21 -> 1.20 (10%) -> 1.11 (50%) -> 0.94 (90%); SAG share 86% -> 63% at 90%, i.e. ~23 percentage points of the corridor stops breaking down - the largest absolute gain because it is the longest, densest corridor. (ii) I-405: 1.43 -> 1.12; SAG 87% -> 77%; still deep in breakdown at 90% - lane additions, not AVs, are the binding constraint here. (iii) I-90: 0.82 -> 0.64; SAG 48% -> 33% - already the healthiest route and improves steadily. (iv) SR-520: 0.93 -> 0.73; SAG 60% -> 20% - the biggest *relative* recovery, consistent with its lower ADT and 4-lane width. Equilibria: yes, two - a free-flow equilibrium stable for VFC < theta and a persistent stop-and-go equilibrium that survives even after demand falls (hysteresis, exchange 1); the transition between them is at VFC = 0.85. Tipping point: the capacity curve g(f) = 0.35*f^2 has no cliff (exchange 3); the *perceived* tipping point in the data is where the f^2 gain finally drags the worst corridors back under theta: the steepest progress between 10% and 50% (I-5 V/C drops 0.09 over that span versus 0.17 from 50% to 90% as more segments clear the threshold), with marginal benefit still positive at 90%. Dedicated lanes: exchange 6 established that dedication is not a safety requirement but a performance measure - it is justified only where platooning can be banked against a persistent bottleneck. The model says that is exactly the ~155-165 milepost core of I-5 (peak ADT 236k-242k, V/C 2.2-2.6 even at f = 0.9) and the worst I-405 segments: there, a dedicated high-occupancy AV lane removes the f^2 penalty of mixed traffic and would be the first lane to flip free. Sensitivity: K-factor 0.08 vs 0.12 shifts I-5 baseline SAG share 86% -> 54% (90%); theta 0.8 vs 0.9 shifts it 93% -> 89%; gain 0.3 vs 0.7 shifts f=0.5 V/C by ~+/-4% - all secondary to the AV fraction itself. Limitations: (a) ADT is a daily aggregate, so the model sizes peak demand with a K-factor rather than measured peak flows - the largest single uncertainty; (b) the segment-wise static model ignores shockwave dynamics, spillback and ramp metering, so it under-states how fast a SAG segment propagates congestion upstream; (c) the f^2 gain law is a penetration-averaged heuristic, not a microscopic platoon-formation model, so it cannot say *where* on a corridor platoons actually form; (d) heavy-vehicle and speed parameters are region-typical values, not measured on these segments; (e) the dropped I-5 6-lane segment, if real, would locally relax the I-5 result by ~1%. Bias: the model slightly *under-states* AV benefit, because it applies the f^2 penalty everywhere (no spatial segregation) and keeps SAG throughput at the conservative 1500 veh/h.
